title: Introduction to Shiny
text:
Shiny lets you turn R code into an interactive web application: the user clicks, chooses and uploads, and R does the computations behind the scenes.
In this course we start from an empty RStudio project and finish with your own app online, with a link you can send to anyone.

title: Your app on GitHub
text:
What the online server needs
To publish the app, the online server (Posit Connect Cloud) takes it from a GitHub repository. So the plan for today is:





flowchart LR
    A["💻 Your project<br/>ui.R + server.R"] --> B["+ app.R<br/>+ manifest.json"]
    B -->|"commit + push"| C["GitHub<br/>repository"]
    C -->|"publish"| D["☁️ Connect Cloud<br/>your app online"]
    style C fill:#24292f,color:#fff
    style D fill:#447099,color:#fff

title: Your app on GitHub
text:
Step 1 · Add app.R
Connect Cloud looks for a primary file, and the standard name for it is app.R. We do not need to rewrite anything: a tiny app.R reads our two files and puts them together.
File → New File → R Script, paste this and save it as app.R in the project folder:
library(shiny)

source("ui.R")        # creates the object ui
source("server.R")    # creates the object server

shinyApp(ui, server)
Run it (Run App): it is the same app as before. Now you can also see why we always wrote ui <- fluidPage(...) and server <- function(...): source() runs the files and leaves those two objects ready for shinyApp().

title: Your app on GitHub
text:
Step 2 · Write the manifest
Connect Cloud is not your computer: it does not know which R packages your app uses. The file manifest.json lists them, with their versions. It is written for you by the rsconnect package.
In the console, with the project open:
# install.packages("rsconnect")   # if you do not have it yet
rsconnect::writeManifest()
A file manifest.json appears in the project. Your folder now looks like this:
my-shiny-app/
├── .gitignore
├── my-shiny-app.Rproj
├── app.R
├── ui.R
├── server.R
└── manifest.json






Re-write the manifest when the packages change



If you later add a package to the app (e.g., library(ggplot2)), run rsconnect::writeManifest() again before pushing, otherwise the online app will not find it.

title: Wait for it: eventReactive()
text:
With reactive(), the app reacts immediately to every change. That is not always what we want:
We want the app to wait until the user says “go”. The “go” is an actionButton(), and the waiting is done by eventReactive().

title: Wait for it: eventReactive()
Wait for it: eventReactive()
Wait for it: eventReactive()
text:
reactive() vs eventReactive()









reactive()
eventReactive()




Re-runs when…
any input it reads changes
only the trigger changes (e.g., a button)


Inputs read inside
are triggers
are only read, at the moment of the trigger


At the start
runs as soon as an output needs it
waits for the first trigger


You use it with
dataInput()
dataInput()








flowchart LR
    D0["input$dataset"] -.->|"read only"| E["dataInput()<br/>eventReactive"]
    B["input$load<br/>(button)"] ==>|"trigger"| E
    E --> G["output$graph"]
    E --> S["output$summary"]
    style D0 fill:#2b6c8e,color:#fff
    style B fill:#d9534f,color:#fff
    style E fill:#f0ad4e,color:#fff
    style G fill:#8fd36f,color:#fff
    style S fill:#8fd36f,color:#fff












And observeEvent()?



You will also find observeEvent(input$button, { ... }). It looks the same, but it returns nothing: it is used to do something (update a menu, show a message, save a file), not to compute a value to use in the outputs. To compute data for the outputs, use eventReactive(). There is an example in Going further.

title: Wait for it: eventReactive()
text:
Your turn






Exercise 1 · In your project



Starting from your reactive() version of the app:

add an actionButton("load", "Select dataset") in the sidebarPanel()
turn reactive({ ... }) into eventReactive(input$load, { ... })

Run the app and check that nothing happens until you click.








Solution 1





See apps/04-eventreactive. Only two lines change compared to the reactive() version:
# ui.R
actionButton("load", "Select dataset")
# server.R
dataInput <- eventReactive(input$load, {
  ...
})
(In that app the choices are named, "rock" = 1, so the server compares input$dataset == 1. With choices = c("rock", "pressure", "cars") you can keep your switch().)









Exercise 2 · Two buttons, two moments



In the live app above, add a second button actionButton("draw", "Draw plot") and make only the plot wait for it, while the summary updates as soon as the data are loaded.
Hint: you need a second eventReactive() that is triggered by input$draw and returns dataInput().








Solution 2





# ui.R, in the sidebarPanel()
actionButton("draw", "Draw plot")
# server.R
plotData <- eventReactive(input$draw, {
  dataInput()
})

output$graph <- renderPlot({
  data <- plotData()
  plot(data[, 1:2])
})
This is the idea of the next page: one button to load the data, one to run the analysis.

title: Outputs and render functions
section: All of them in one app
text:
All of them in one app
The same dataset, shown four ways. Change the dataset and the number of rows.
#| '!! shinylive warning !!': |
#|   shinylive does not work in self-contained HTML documents.
#|   Please set `embed-resources: false` in your metadata.
#| standalone: true
#| components: [editor, viewer]
#| layout: vertical
#| viewerHeight: 900
## file: ui.R
library(shiny)

ui <- fluidPage(
  sidebarLayout(
    sidebarPanel(
      selectInput("dataset", "Choose a dataset:",
                  choices = c("rock", "pressure", "cars")),
      sliderInput("n", "Rows in the table:", min = 1, max = 10, value = 5)
    ),
    mainPanel(
      h4("textOutput()"),
      textOutput("text"),
      h4("verbatimTextOutput()"),
      verbatimTextOutput("print"),
      h4("tableOutput()"),
      tableOutput("table"),
      h4("plotOutput()"),
      plotOutput("plot", height = "300px")
    )
  )
)
## file: server.R
library(shiny)

server <- function(input, output, session) {

  output$text <- renderText({
    data <- get(input$dataset)
    paste("The dataset", input$dataset, "has", nrow(data), "rows and",
          ncol(data), "columns.")
  })

  output$print <- renderPrint({
    data <- get(input$dataset)
    summary(data)
  })

  output$table <- renderTable({
    data <- get(input$dataset)
    head(data, input$n)
  })

  output$plot <- renderPlot({
    data <- get(input$dataset)
    plot(data[, 1:2])
  })
}
get("cars") returns the object called cars: it is a quick way to go from the name of a dataset (a text, the value of the input) to the dataset itself.

title: Outputs and render functions
text:
renderText() or renderPrint()?
They look similar but they are not the same:

renderText() turns the result into one plain string (it uses cat()): good for sentences
renderPrint() shows the result as the R console would print it: good for summary(), str(), models, data frames

In the app above, replace renderPrint with renderText for summary(data) (and verbatimTextOutput with textOutput in the UI): the numbers are all glued together. That is why we use renderPrint() for statistical output.

title: Outputs and render functions
text:
Common mistakes






When the box stays empty




The IDs do not match: plotOutput("graph") in the UI, output$grahp in the server. No error, just an empty box
The pair is wrong: plotOutput() in the UI, renderPrint() in the server. The box cannot show that content
You forgot output$...: renderPlot({ ... }) alone computes the plot and throws it away
The box is not in the UI: the server fills output$summary, but ui.R has no ...Output("summary")

title: Outputs and render functions
text:
Your turn






Exercise 1 · From one output to two



Open the first datasets app in the editor and add a second plot: a histogram of the first column of the dataset (hist(data[, 1])).
You need two changes: one in ui.R and one in server.R.








Solution 1





# ui.R, inside mainPanel()
plotOutput("hist", height = "300px")
# server.R, inside the server function
output$hist <- renderPlot({
  data <- get(input$dataset)
  hist(data[, 1], main = names(data)[1])
})

title: How Shiny thinks
text: The Shiny page showed the logic: the UI sets the options and displays the results, the server elaborates the options and sends back the results. Here we look inside the two pieces, and at how they talk to each other.

title: How Shiny thinks
section: The UI is a web page

title: How Shiny thinks
text:
The server is a function
server <- function(input, output, session) {
  ...
}
Shiny calls this function once for each user that opens the app (each user has their own session). Inside it:

input is a list with the current value of every input, accessed by ID: input$mySelection. You can read it, you cannot change it
output is the list of the boxes to fill, accessed by ID: output$myOutput <- render…({ … })

title: How Shiny thinks
text:
The contract: IDs
Let’s go back to the first app and follow the IDs:
# ui.R
ui <- fluidPage(
1  selectInput(inputId = "mySelection",
2              label = h3("Select box"),
3              choices = list("Choice 1" = 1, "Choice 2" = 2, "Choice 3" = 3),
4              selected = 1),
5  verbatimTextOutput(outputId = "myOutput")
)

1

The ID of the input: for internal use, the server will call it input$mySelection

2

The label: for external use, it is what the user reads

3

The options: the user sees "Choice 1", the server receives "1" (as text!)

4

The option selected when the app starts

5

The ID of an empty output box: the server will fill output$myOutput


# server.R
server <- function(input, output, session) {
1  output$myOutput <- renderPrint({
2    paste("This is my choice:", input$mySelection)
  })
}

1

Fill the box myOutput. renderPrint() is the partner of verbatimTextOutput()

2

Read the current value of the input mySelection







flowchart LR
    A["UI<br/>selectInput(inputId = 'mySelection')"] -->|"input$mySelection"| B["SERVER<br/>renderPrint({ ... })"]
    B -->|"output$myOutput"| C["UI<br/>verbatimTextOutput(outputId = 'myOutput')"]
    style A fill:#2b6c8e,color:#fff
    style C fill:#2b6c8e,color:#fff
    style B fill:#8fd36f,color:#fff







The rules of the contract

Defined in the UI, not used in the server: nothing happens. The widget is there, you can play with it, but nobody is listening
Used in the server, not defined in the UI (often a typo!): Shiny does not warn you

input$myselection (lowercase s) simply is NULL, so the result is empty or the code fails
output$myOuptut is computed but never shown, because no box has that name

IDs must be unique: two elements with the same ID make the app behave unpredictably (outputs may not show at all)
input is read-only: input$mySelection <- 2 is an error



Spot the bug
This app has a bug: the output never shows the choice. Find it and fix it in the editor, then press ▶.
#| '!! shinylive warning !!': |
#|   shinylive does not work in self-contained HTML documents.
#|   Please set `embed-resources: false` in your metadata.
#| standalone: true
#| components: [editor, viewer]
#| layout: vertical
#| viewerHeight: 220
## file: ui.R
library(shiny)

ui <- fluidPage(
  selectInput(
    inputId = "mySelection",
    label = h3("Select box"),
    choices = list("Choice 1" = 1, "Choice 2" = 2, "Choice 3" = 3),
    selected = 1
  ),
  verbatimTextOutput(outputId = "myOutput")
)
## file: server.R
library(shiny)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  output$myOutput <- renderPrint({
    paste("This is my choice:", input$myselection)
  })
}






Solution





input$myselection must be input$mySelection: IDs are case-sensitive. Since input$myselection does not exist, it is NULL, and paste() silently ignores it.

title: How Shiny thinks
text:
Reactivity: the mental model
Look at the server again: there is no loop, no “when the user clicks, do this”. How does the output know it has to change?
Think of a spreadsheet. If cell B1 contains =A1 * 2, you never “run” B1: every time A1 changes, B1 updates by itself.
render*() functions work the same way:

the code inside render*({ ... }) is a recipe, not a command executed once
Shiny notes which inputs the recipe reads (here: input$mySelection)
when one of those inputs changes, Shiny re-runs the recipe and sends the new result to the box






flowchart LR
    I["input$mySelection<br/>changes"] --> R["renderPrint({ ... })<br/>runs again"] --> O["output$myOutput<br/>is updated"]
    style I fill:#2b6c8e,color:#fff
    style R fill:#8fd36f,color:#fff
    style O fill:#2b6c8e,color:#fff






This is why the server is not read from top to bottom like a script: each recipe runs when it needs to.






Inputs live only inside reactive code



Reading an input outside a recipe does not work:
server <- function(input, output, session) {
  choice <- input$mySelection        # ❌ outside render*()
  output$myOutput <- renderPrint({ choice })
}
Error: Can't access reactive value 'mySelection' outside of reactive consumer.
The server function runs once, at the start: at that moment nobody has chosen anything yet. Inputs must be read inside render*() (or the other reactive functions we will meet: reactive(), eventReactive()).








In a nutshell




UI = what the user sees: inputs (controls) and outputs (empty boxes)
Server = a function of input and output that fills the boxes
They talk only through IDs: inputId → input$id, outputId → output$id
render*() are recipes that re-run automatically when the inputs they read change

title: Shiny
text:
ui (User Interface)
The container, whatever sees the user
Used for setting the desired configurations of options that will be elaborated in the server
Used for displaying the results of the computations that took place in the server


server
It gets the work done, according to the configuration set in the UI
Replaces the results into the allocated spaces


UI and Server work in a flow, communicating to each other (Figure 1).









flowchart LR

    UI["**UI**<br/><br/>Set the options<br/>Displays the results"]
    SERVER["**SERVER**<br/><br/>Elaborates the options<br/>Sends back the results"]

    UI -->|"Input"| SERVER
    SERVER -->|"Output"| UI

    style UI fill:#2b6c8e,stroke:#1b4258,stroke-width:2px,color:#ffffff
    style SERVER fill:#8fd36f,stroke:#4c8b3a,stroke-width:2px,color:#ffffff

    linkStyle default stroke:#FFD700,stroke-width:5px









Figure 1: Interaction between the user interface (UI) and the server.




Define something in the ui and not using it in the server: nothing happens, it just doesn’t exist
Calling something in the server that has not been defined in the ui: it doesn’t exist either, so you get errors everywhere or, even worse, nothing at all, without any warning (Spot the bug)

In the next page we put this same app in an RStudio project, with the ui in a script called ui.R and the server in a script called server.R.

title: A Shiny project
text:
A Shiny app is a folder. In the folder there are (at least) two R scripts:
The best way to keep that folder tidy is an RStudio project. It will also be the folder that we put on GitHub and online on Day 2, so we create it right away.

title: A Shiny project
text:
Step 1 · Create the project
In RStudio:

File → New Project… → New Directory → New Project
Directory name: my-shiny-app (no spaces, no accents)
Choose where to save it (e.g., Documents/GitHub) and click Create Project

RStudio opens the project: the Files pane shows the folder, which now contains only my-shiny-app.Rproj.






Why a project?




The project folder is the app: everything the app needs lives there
File paths are relative to the project, so the app works on any computer
On Day 2 the very same folder becomes a GitHub repository and then goes online

title: A Shiny project
text:
Step 2 · Create ui.R and server.R

File → New File → R Script, then save it (File → Save) as ui.R
File → New File → R Script, then save it as server.R

The names must be exactly ui.R and server.R (lowercase, capital R), and both files must be in the same folder.
Your project now looks like this:
my-shiny-app/
├── my-shiny-app.Rproj
├── ui.R
└── server.R






Alternative: let RStudio write the two scripts





File → New File → Shiny Web App… → Application type: Multiple File (ui.R/server.R).
RStudio creates a sub-folder with the name you give to the application, containing a ui.R and a server.R with a demo app (a histogram of the Old Faithful geyser). It works, but the app ends up one folder deeper than the project. In this course we keep ui.R and server.R directly in the project folder.

title: A Shiny project
text:
Step 3 · Write the two scripts
Copy this into ui.R:
library(shiny)

ui <- fluidPage(
  selectInput(
    inputId = "mySelection",            # name used by the server
    label = h3("Select box"),           # what the user reads
    choices = list("Choice 1" = 1, "Choice 2" = 2, "Choice 3" = 3),
    selected = 1
  ),
  verbatimTextOutput(outputId = "myOutput")  # empty box, filled by the server
)
and this into server.R:
library(shiny)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  output$myOutput <- renderPrint({
    paste("This is my choice:", input$mySelection)
  })
}
We dissect every line in the next page. For now, notice two things:

ui.R creates one object, ui: the page
server.R creates one object, server: a function of input and output

title: A Shiny project
text:
Step 4 · Run the app
As soon as a file called ui.R or server.R is open, RStudio replaces the usual Run button with ▶ Run App. Click it.
What happens:

In the console you read something like Listening on http://127.0.0.1:4321: R has started a small web server on your computer
A window (or a browser tab) opens with the app: that is the UI, turned into a web page
The console shows a red stop sign: R is busy serving the app, so you cannot use the console until you stop it

Choose another option in the menu: the text changes. Every time you change the input, the browser tells R, R runs the code in the server and sends back the new result.
To stop the app, click the red stop sign in the console (or press EscEsc in the console). If you change the code while the app is running, click Reload app in the app window.






The most common problems at this stage




No Run App button → the file is not saved, or it is not called exactly ui.R/server.R
could not find function "fluidPage" → library(shiny) is missing, or shiny is not installed
The console does not respond → the app is still running: stop it first

title: A Shiny project
text:
Two files or one file?
Shiny also accepts a single file called app.R that contains both pieces and ends with shinyApp():
library(shiny)

ui <- fluidPage(...)                              # what was in ui.R
server <- function(input, output, session) {...}  # what was in server.R

shinyApp(ui, server)                              # put them together
It is the same app. We use two files because they make the logic visible: one script for what the user sees, one for what R does. On Day 2 we will add a tiny app.R that simply reads the two files, because that is what the online server looks for.






Checkpoint



✅ A project my-shiny-app with ui.R and server.R ✅ Run App opens the app ✅ You know how to stop it

title: Input widgets
text:
Every input widget has the same first two arguments:
What changes from widget to widget is what arrives in input$id: a number, a text, a vector, a date, a data frame… Knowing it is what saves you from most errors in the server.
In all the apps on this page, the server prints the class and the structure (str()) of each input, so you can see exactly what it receives. Play with the widgets and watch the boxes on the right.

text:

ui <- fluidPage(
  fluidRow(
    column(6, selectInput("sel", "selectInput()",
                          choices = c("rock", "pressure", "cars"))),
    column(6, verbatimTextOutput("sel_out"))
  ),
  fluidRow(
    column(6, selectInput("sel_named", "selectInput() with named choices",
                          choices = c("rock" = 1, "pressure" = 2, "cars" = 3))),
    column(6, verbatimTextOutput("sel_named_out"))
  ),
  fluidRow(
    column(6, selectInput("sel_multi", "selectInput(multiple = TRUE)",
                          choices = c("A", "B", "C"), multiple = TRUE)),
    column(6, verbatimTextOutput("sel_multi_out"))
  ),
  fluidRow(
    column(6, radioButtons("radio", "radioButtons()",
                           choices = c("Low" = "low", "High" = "high"))),
    column(6, verbatimTextOutput("radio_out"))
  ),
  fluidRow(
    column(6, checkboxGroupInput("group", "checkboxGroupInput()",
                                 choices = c("A", "B", "C"))),
    column(6, verbatimTextOutput("group_out"))
  )
)
## file: server.R
library(shiny)

# helper: print the class and the structure of an object
inspect <- function(x) {
  cat("class:", class(x), "\n")
  str(x)
}

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  output$sel_out       <- renderPrint(inspect(input$sel))
  output$sel_named_out <- renderPrint(inspect(input$sel_named))
  output$sel_multi_out <- renderPrint(inspect(input$sel_multi))
  output$radio_out     <- renderPrint(inspect(input$radio))
  output$group_out     <- renderPrint(inspect(input$group))
}






Things to notice




With named choices ("rock" = 1) the user sees the name, the server receives the value, and the value is always text: "1", not 1
multiple = TRUE and checkboxGroupInput() return a vector, and NULL when nothing is selected

Widget

## file: ui.R
library(shiny)

ui <- fluidPage(
  sidebarLayout(
    sidebarPanel(
      selectInput(
        inputId = "dataset",
        label = "Choose a dataset:",
        choices = c("rock", "pressure", "cars")
      )
    ),
    mainPanel(
      plotOutput("graph"),
      verbatimTextOutput("summary")
    )
  )
)

## file: server.R
library(shiny)

server <- function(input, output, session) {

  output$graph <- renderPlot({
    data <- switch(input$dataset,       # the same code...
                   rock = rock,
                   pressure = pressure,
                   cars = cars)
    plot(data[, 1:2])
  })

  output$summary <- renderPrint({
    data <- switch(input$dataset,       # ...written twice
                   rock = rock,
                   pressure = pressure,
                   cars = cars)
    summary(data[, 1:2])
  })
}

It works, but look at the server: the switch() that picks the dataset is written twice, once in each render*().

If you add a dataset, you must remember to change it in two places
Every time the input changes, the same data are prepared twice: with a big file or a slow computation, the app becomes slow

title: Reactivity and reactive()
text:
The solution: reactive()
reactive() creates a reactive expression: a recipe that returns a value and that the outputs can share.
server <- function(input, output, session) {

1  dataInput <- reactive({
    switch(input$dataset,
           rock = rock,
           pressure = pressure,
           cars = cars)
  })

  output$graph <- renderPlot({
2    data <- dataInput()
    plot(data[, 1:2])
  })

  output$summary <- renderPrint({
    data <- dataInput()
    summary(data[, 1:2])
  })
}

1

Write the recipe once. It reads input$dataset, so it reacts to it

2

Call it, like a function: dataInput(), with the parentheses


#| '!! shinylive warning !!': |
#|   shinylive does not work in self-contained HTML documents.
#|   Please set `embed-resources: false` in your metadata.
#| standalone: true
#| components: [editor, viewer]
#| layout: vertical
#| viewerHeight: 650
## file: ui.R
library(shiny)

ui <- fluidPage(
  sidebarLayout(
    sidebarPanel(
      selectInput(
        inputId = "dataset",
        label = "Choose a dataset:",
        choices = c("rock", "pressure", "cars")
      )
    ),
    mainPanel(
      plotOutput("graph"),
      verbatimTextOutput("summary")
    )
  )
)

## file: server.R
library(shiny)

server <- function(input, output, session) {

  # written once, used everywhere
  dataInput <- reactive({
    switch(input$dataset,
           rock = rock,
           pressure = pressure,
           cars = cars)
  })

  output$graph <- renderPlot({
    data <- dataInput()                 # note the ()
    plot(data[, 1:2])
  })

  output$summary <- renderPrint({
    data <- dataInput()
    summary(data[, 1:2])
  })
}

Now the chain of reactions is:





flowchart LR
    I["input$dataset"] --> D["dataInput()"]
    D --> G["output$graph"]
    D --> S["output$summary"]
    style I fill:#2b6c8e,color:#fff
    style D fill:#f0ad4e,color:#fff
    style G fill:#8fd36f,color:#fff
    style S fill:#8fd36f,color:#fff






When input$dataset changes, dataInput() is recomputed once, and both outputs use the new value. If nothing changed, calling dataInput() again just returns the value already computed (Shiny caches it).






Three things to remember about reactive()




Parentheses: dataInput() is the value, dataInput (without parentheses) is the recipe itself. plot(dataInput[, 1:2]) is an error
A reactive expression can only be called inside reactive code (render*(), another reactive()…), exactly like input$...
It is lazy: it runs only if some output needs it

title: Reactivity and reactive()
section: Only what depends on a change re-runs
text:
Only what depends on a change re-runs
Shiny knows exactly who reads what. In this app each output prints the time it was last computed. Move the slider: which outputs are recomputed? And when you change the dataset?

## file: ui.R
library(shiny)

ui <- fluidPage(
  sidebarLayout(
    sidebarPanel(
      selectInput("dataset", "Choose a dataset:",
                  choices = c("rock", "pressure", "cars")),
      sliderInput("n", "Rows to show:", min = 1, max = 10, value = 3)
    ),

      h4("Summary (uses only the dataset)"),
      verbatimTextOutput("summary"),
      h4("First rows (uses the dataset AND the slider)"),
      verbatimTextOutput("rows")
    )
  )
)
## file: server.R
library(shiny)

now <- function() format(Sys.time(), "%H:%M:%OS2")

server <- function(input, output, session) {

  dataInput <- reactive({
    get(input$dataset)
  })

  output$summary <- renderPrint({
    cat("computed at", now(), "\n\n")
    summary(dataInput())
  })

  output$rows <- renderPrint({
    cat("computed at", now(), "\n\n")
    head(dataInput(), input$n)
  })
}

    style D fill:#f0ad4e,color:#fff
    style S fill:#8fd36f,color:#fff

title: Deploy on Connect Cloud
text:
Several servers can host a Shiny app (overview by Posit). You can also build your own server from scratch, for instance following Dean Attali’s guide, but that requires some system administration.
We use Posit Connect Cloud: it is free for public apps and publishes directly from GitHub. (You may also find shinyapps.io, the older Posit service: the logic is the same, but here we use Connect Cloud.)

title: Deploy on Connect Cloud
text:
Several servers can host a Shiny app (overview by Posit). You can also build your own server from scratch, for instance following Dean Attali’s guide, but that requires some system administration.
We use Posit Connect Cloud: it is free for public apps and publishes directly from GitHub. (You may also find shinyapps.io, the older Posit service: the logic is the same, but here we use Connect Cloud.)

title: Deploy on Connect Cloud
text:
Step 1 · The account
Sign up on Connect Cloud and choose to sign in with GitHub, so that Connect Cloud can see your repositories.



Connect Cloud landing page and account creation





Link Connect Cloud to your GitHub account


Follow the instructions and choose an account name.

title: Deploy on Connect Cloud
text:
Step 2 · Publish

From the Home of your profile, click Publish
Choose Shiny
Select the repository (my-shiny-app), the branch (main) and the primary file: app.R
Click Publish and wait: Connect Cloud installs R and the packages listed in manifest.json, then starts the app




Deploy the app and publish it


When it is done, you get a link: that is your app, online. Open it from your phone, send it to a friend.

title: Deploy on Connect Cloud
text:
Step 3 · Update the app
The online app is a copy of what is on GitHub. To change it:

edit the app in RStudio and check it with Run App
if you added packages: rsconnect::writeManifest()
commit + push with GitHub Desktop
on Connect Cloud, republish the content

title: Deploy on Connect Cloud
text:
When something goes wrong






Troubleshooting




The repository is not in the list → it is private, or Connect Cloud does not have access to it: check the GitHub permissions of Connect Cloud
“No manifest” / missing dependencies → manifest.json is not in the repository: write it and push it
The app works on your computer but not online → open the logs of the content on Connect Cloud: they show the R error. Common causes:

a package used in the app but not in the manifest (re-run writeManifest())
a file read with an absolute path (C:/Users/...): use paths relative to the project
a file (data, images) that is on your computer but was not committed

The app starts but an output is empty → it is a Shiny problem, not a deploy problem: go back to the rules of the contract









🎉 Done



Your app is online. From here, Going further shows how to improve it: better layouts, interactive plots, downloads.

title: Layouts
text: fluidPage() is a page based on a grid 12 units wide. On top of it, Shiny offers a few ready-made structures.

title: Layouts
text:
Try them
#| '!! shinylive warning !!': |
#|   shinylive does not work in self-contained HTML documents.
#|   Please set `embed-resources: false` in your metadata.
#| standalone: true
#| components: [editor, viewer]
#| layout: vertical
#| viewerHeight: 650
## file: ui.R
library(shiny)

ui <- fluidPage(
  titlePanel("Layouts"),
  sidebarLayout(
    sidebarPanel(
      selectInput("dataset", "Choose a dataset:",
                  choices = c("rock", "pressure", "cars")),
      width = 3                       # the sidebar takes 3 of 12 units
    ),
    mainPanel(
      tabsetPanel(
        tabPanel("Plot", plotOutput("plot")),
        tabPanel("Summary", verbatimTextOutput("summary")),
        tabPanel("Two columns",
                 fluidRow(
                   column(6, h4("First column"), tableOutput("head")),
                   column(6, h4("Second column"), plotOutput("hist", height = "250px"))
                 ))
      ),
      width = 9
    )
  )
)
## file: server.R
library(shiny)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  dataInput <- reactive(get(input$dataset))

  output$plot    <- renderPlot(plot(dataInput()[, 1:2]))
  output$summary <- renderPrint(summary(dataInput()))
  output$head    <- renderTable(head(dataInput()))
  output$hist    <- renderPlot(hist(dataInput()[, 1], main = names(dataInput())[1]))
}






Exercise



Move the dataset menu out of the sidebar and put it in a fluidRow() on top of the tabs. Change the widths of the two columns to 4 and 8.


More layouts (navbar pages, cards, dashboards with bslib) in the Shiny layout gallery.

title: Updating inputs
text:
In Your app: explore a dataset the X and Y menus were created by the server with renderUI(). There is another way: the menus exist in ui.R from the start, empty, and the server updates their choices when the data are loaded.
Every input has its update*() function: updateSliderInput(), updateTextInput(), updateNumericInput()…

title: Updating inputs
section: req(): wait for what you need
text:
req(): wait for what you need
In this app analysisInput() starts with req(input$x, input$y). req() checks that its arguments are “available” (not NULL, not empty, not FALSE…). If they are not, it stops the computation silently: no red error, the output simply waits.
Use it whenever an output needs something that may not be there yet: an uploaded file, a selection, a click.
